Researchers are studying the sequence of events in ischemic myocardium.  The left circumflex artery of an anesthetized laboratory animal is completely occluded, and intracellular ATP and lactate concentrations in the ischemic myocardial cells are measured continuously.  The results are shown below.

 

Which of the following events is most likely to occur first in these myocardial cells?​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌
explanation:
Total myocardial ischemia halts oxidative phosphorylation within seconds, forcing cardiomyocytes to rely on anaerobic glycolysis, which generates lactate but cannot meet their energy needs.  Creatine phosphate is rapidly consumed to regenerate ATP, initially preserving cellular ATP levels.  However, continued ATP hydrolysis causes inorganic phosphate to accumulate, while lactic acid production and the lack of washout cause intracellular acidosis.  Increased inorganic phosphate and hydrogen ions impair myofilament force generation, causing loss of contractility within approximately 60 seconds, before ATP is substantially depleted.

As ischemia persists and ATP levels continue to fall, ATP-dependent ion pumps (eg, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) fail, allowing sodium and water to accumulate in the cell and causing cellular and mitochondrial swelling over the following minutes (Choice D).  These early changes, including the loss of contractility, are reversible if blood flow is restored promptly.

However, continued ischemia causes progressive ATP degradation to ADP, AMP, and eventually adenosine, which diffuses out of cardiomyocytes.  This depletes the adenine nucleotide pool and limits ATP replenishment even after blood flow is restored.  Irreversible injury can begin after approximately 20–30 minutes of total ischemia as severe energy depletion, calcium overload (from impaired Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange and failure of ATP-dependent calcium pumps), and membrane damage disrupt cellular homeostasis.  Loss of sarcolemmal integrity permits further calcium influx and leakage of intracellular proteins (eg, troponin) into the circulation (Choices B and E).

(Choice C)  Oxygen free radicals are generated mainly during reperfusion, when oxygen is reintroduced to ischemic myocardium; in this experiment, the artery remains occluded.  Together with calcium overload, this oxidative burst contributes to myocardial stunning, a transient contractile dysfunction that persists after blood flow is restored to viable myocardium.  Contractility typically recovers over hours to days.

Educational objective:Total myocardial ischemia causes loss of contractility within approximately 60 seconds, before substantial ATP depletion or structural injury.  Early reperfusion can salvage myocardium, although transient contractile dysfunction (myocardial stunning) may persist.  With continued ischemia, irreversible injury can begin after approximately 20–30 minutes as severe energy depletion and membrane damage develop.​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌
